query: Why did the pH at Seaview Outfall Buoy crash to 3 on September 27?

response.answer:
The pH at Seaview Outfall Buoy did not crash to 3 on September 27 — that reading was a sensor fault, not a measurement.

Here's what the data shows for that day:

- The lowest valid pH reading on September 27 was **7.862** (23 valid readings).
- There was one reading of **2.07** at 2026-09-27T23:48:57Z, but the device excluded it as physically impossible — it's outside the pH range natural water can reach (roughly pH 3–12), which points to a probe failure rather than a real change in the water 【T1】.

So the "crash to 3" you may have seen was actually that faulty 2.07 reading. A single isolated point like this is more likely a sensor or connection problem than a real water-quality change — a real event more often shows a combination of readings that fits a physical explanation and lasts across several readings.

One more thing worth noting: the device operates in salt water, but the deployment's configured water type is freshwater — you may want to check that configuration.

If the pH probe keeps producing impossible readings, it's worth inspecting it for fouling or damage, and contacting Clean Earth Rovers support (sales@cleanearthrovers.com) if it looks damaged or the problem persists.

20 	Chapter A6.0. Guidelines for Field-Measured Water-Quality Properties
Step 1
Test, calibrate, and check field instruments.
Step 2
Purge well; see text for exceptions and instructions.
Step 3
Collect sample in compositing device using clean-hands/dirty-hands procedures. Lower
sampler smoothly to desired depth; raise sampler smoothly at a constant rate, keeping
lines clean and off the ground. Place sampler in holding stand.
Step 4
Withdraw subsamples from sampler. Attach clean bottom-emptying device if using a bailer.
Filter inline to bottle/measurement vessel. Drain subsample without turbulence into
bottles/vessel. Rinse bottle three times with sample (filtrate for filtured samples), fill to top,
cap tightly, and maintain at temperature of source until measurment.
Step 5
Rinse sensors, measurement vessels, and other apparatus three times
with sample. Rinse with deionized water for alkalinity measurement.
Step 6
Pour sample into measurement vessel; insert sensor(s).
• 	Allow sensors to equilibrate to sample temperature.
• 	Do not allow sensors to touch bottom or sides of vessel.
Step 7
Swirl or stir gently.
• 	Minimize vortex; keep sensors out of vortex.
• 	For pH measurement, do not stir samples having conductivity less than 100 μS/cm.
• 	When using magnetic stir bar, use smallest stir bar.
Step 8
Record field measurement and procedures on field forms.
• 	Record median value of stabilized readings (see table 6.0-1).
• 	If readings do not stabilize, incease number of measurements and record last five or more sequential readings.
• 	If there is a consistent trend toward lower or higher values, record the first value, the range of values, and the time
period observed.
Step 9
Repeat from step 6 on two or more subsamples from the same sample volume
to document precision. Rinse sensors thoroughly with deionized water.

Operating principle
A pH (potential of Hydrogen) probe measures the hydrogen ion activity in a liquid.
At the tip of a pH probe is a glass membrane. This glass membrane permits hydrogen
ions from the liquid being measured to defuse into the outer layer of the glass, while
larger ions remain in the solution. The difference in the concentration of hydrogen ions
(outside the probe vs. inside the probe) creates a VERY small current. This current
is proportional to the concentration of hydrogen ions in the liquid being measured.

-- 10 of 24 --2.0 Equipment and Supplies 	3
for the determination of water temperature, specific electrical
conductance (SC), pH, dissolved-oxygen (DO) concentration
and turbidity are commonly bundled in sondes used for USGS
water-quality studies. Permanent sensors for measuring baro-
metric pressure (for use with a DO sensor), water depth (either
vented or unvented), and location (global positioning systems)
either are standard equipment with many multiparameter
instruments or can be added at extra cost. Nonpermanent
sensors for measuring oxidation-reduction potential (Eh), fluo-
rescence1, velocity, and concentrations of nitrate, ammonia,
ammonium, chloride, and chlorophyll can be added to many
sondes through use of sensor ports. The types and number of
sensors that can be bundled in a given sonde depend on the
number of ports available in an instrument model, typically
four to seven. When selecting a sensor, consult the manufac-
turer’s recommendations and specifications for the instrument,
taking into consideration the environmental conditions to be
encountered, the data-quality objectives of the study, and the
specific benefit of a particular sensor technology that could be
applicable to the anticipated field conditions.
Table 6.8–2 lists the equipment specifications required
when making field measurements with a multiparameter
instrument. Table 6.8–3 lists the specifications for calibration
1Fluorescence sensors indicate different algal pigment concentrations; see
NFM chapter A7.4 and Booth and others (2023) for additional information.
solutions required when using multiparameter instruments.
The requirements in tables 6.8–2 and 6.8–3 may be modified
to fit specific project needs. Ancillary supplies and equipment
needed to measure field properties with multiparameter instru-
ments (table 6.8–4) are the same as or similar to those required
for the calibration and maintenance of single-parameter
instruments, and are discussed in detail in the individual field-
measurement chapters (NFM chapters A6.1 through A6.7).
2.1 Equipment Transport
Multiparameter instruments have become more robust
with time, but the sensors can easily be damaged if handled
improperly. Some sensors require storage and transporta-
tion in a wet/moist environment, whereas others do not,
check the manufacturer’s recommendations. Sondes should
not be exposed to extreme heat or cold. Transport in a case
that is designed to protect the equipment following the
manufacturer’s recommendations is best. For transportation
and storage, use a padded case that protects the sonde from
shock. The padding should be of a type that will not absorb
water. Hard-sided cases should be equipped with a vent so
that internal pressure can equalize with that of the atmosphere.
Do not expose the case to direct sunlight in order to avoid
solar heating of the equipment inside.
